prompt: Which market structure is imperfectly competitive?

options.label: A
options.text: A market with no market power

options.label: C
options.text: A market in which each firm faces perfectly elastic demand

options.label: D
options.text: A market in which every firm is a price taker

explanation: Monopolistically competitive firms sell differentiated products and have some control over price. This makes the market imperfectly competitive.

prompt: Which of the following is included among imperfectly competitive product markets?

options.label: E
options.text: A market with no barriers and no market power

explanation: Oligopoly contains a few interdependent firms with market power. It is an imperfectly competitive product market.

prompt: Which factor-market structure is identified as imperfectly competitive in the CED?

options.label: C
options.text: A market with perfectly elastic firm demand

explanation: Monopsony gives a buyer market power in purchasing inputs. It is an imperfectly competitive factor market.

prompt: A firm in an imperfectly competitive output market generally faces

options.label: D
options.text: A market supply curve as its demand curve

options.label: E
options.text: A perfectly vertical demand curve by definition

explanation: A lower price is needed to attract additional purchases from the firm's customers. Its demand curve therefore slopes downward.

prompt: If an imperfectly competitive firm wants to sell more output, all else equal, it must

options.label: C
options.text: Keep price unchanged in every case

explanation: The firm faces an inverse relationship between its selling price and sales. Selling more requires lowering price.

prompt: A defining sign of inefficiency in an imperfectly competitive market is

options.label: B
options.text: Marginal cost greater than price in every case

options.label: D
options.text: Average fixed cost equal to price

explanation: Price above marginal cost means consumers value additional output more than it costs to produce. This indicates allocative inefficiency.

prompt: When price exceeds marginal cost, the market output is generally

options.label: C
options.text: Above the allocatively efficient quantity in every case

explanation: Additional units with value above marginal cost would add net benefits. Not producing them leaves gains from trade unrealized.

prompt: Which is an example of a barrier to entry?
explanation: Large start-up expenses require substantial resources before a rival can operate. They can deter entry and protect existing firms' market power.

prompt: Which is an example of a legal barrier to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: An increase in the number of buyers

explanation: Licenses and legal restrictions limit who can enter. They can reduce competition from new firms.

prompt: Exclusive ownership of a key resource can sustain imperfect competition because it

options.label: B
options.text: Forces price to equal marginal cost

explanation: A rival cannot produce readily without access to the essential input. Exclusive control of it can block entry.

prompt: Barriers to entry tend to

options.label: C
options.text: Force all firms to sell identical products

options.label: D
options.text: Make every firm a price taker

explanation: Barriers make it harder for rivals to enter and challenge incumbent firms. Market power can therefore persist.

prompt: Which market is most consistent with imperfect competition?

options.label: A
options.text: A market in which each firm must accept the market price

options.label: B
options.text: A market with a horizontal firm demand curve and no barriers

options.label: C
options.text: A market with no influence over price by any seller

options.label: D
options.text: A market in which P always equals MC

options.label: E
options.text: A market in which individual firms have some market power

explanation: Imperfectly competitive firms have some influence over market outcomes. They do not simply accept price as pure price takers do.

prompt: An imperfectly competitive firm's demand curve slopes downward primarily because
explanation: Consumers purchase more from the firm only at a lower price. This creates a downward-sloping individual demand curve.

prompt: If price is greater than marginal cost, producing one more unit at the margin would
explanation: The extra unit's benefit exceeds its production cost. Producing it would increase total surplus.

prompt: Which condition is consistent with allocative efficiency?

options.label: C
options.text: Price is unrelated to marginal cost

options.label: E
options.text: Price must equal average fixed cost

explanation: P = MC equates the marginal buyer's valuation with marginal production cost. It is the allocatively efficient benchmark.

prompt: Which is NOT an imperfectly competitive product-market structure?

options.label: B
options.text: A product market with market power

explanation: Perfect competition has price-taking firms. It is the competitive benchmark used to compare imperfect market structures.

prompt: A large required up-front investment before production begins is best classified as
explanation: High fixed or start-up expenses create a financial hurdle for entrants. Potential rivals may be unable or unwilling to commit those resources.

prompt: A patent that legally prevents rivals from producing a protected invention is best understood as
explanation: Legal protections can prevent competing sellers from entering. They can sustain the protected firm's market power.

prompt: If one firm controls the only commercially usable deposit of a required mineral, the situation illustrates

options.label: A
options.text: Exclusive control of a key resource

explanation: Owning an indispensable resource can deny rivals an input they need. This creates a barrier to entry.

prompt: The graph shows two individual firms. Which firm is more consistent with imperfect competition?

options.label: C
options.text: Both firms equally, because both face horizontal demand

options.label: D
options.text: Firm A only because its price is constant

options.label: E
options.text: Neither firm, because imperfect firms cannot have demand curves

explanation: Firm B must lower price to increase sales along its downward-sloping demand curve. This is consistent with some market power.

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an imperfectly competitive firm from a perfectly competitive firm?

options.label: A
options.text: The perfectly competitive firm faces downward-sloping demand

options.label: B
options.text: The perfectly competitive firm always has barriers to entry

options.label: C
options.text: The imperfectly competitive firm always produces at P=MC

options.label: D
options.text: The imperfectly competitive firm always has zero profit

options.label: E
options.text: It can influence its selling price

explanation: Imperfect competition allows some market power. Perfect competition instead makes each firm a price taker.

prompt: In an imperfectly competitive market, prices may fail to coordinate all mutually beneficial transactions because

options.label: E
options.text: Price must always equal marginal cost

explanation: When price exceeds marginal cost, additional output can be worth more than it costs. The market can therefore produce less than the efficient quantity.

prompt: Which change would most directly weaken a barrier to entry?

options.label: B
options.text: Granting exclusive control of an essential input

options.label: C
options.text: Strengthening a legal prohibition on entry

explanation: Removing a legal restriction lets more potential rivals enter. It weakens that barrier to entry.

prompt: Which change would most directly strengthen a barrier to entry?

options.label: B
options.text: Opening access to a formerly exclusive resource

explanation: A costly legal requirement adds an expense or obstacle before a firm can operate. Entry becomes more difficult.

prompt: If a firm can sell 10 units at $20 each but must charge $18 to sell 11 units, the firm is behaving like

options.label: C
options.text: A firm facing perfectly elastic demand

options.label: D
options.text: A firm with no influence over price

options.label: E
options.text: A firm in a market where P must equal MC

explanation: The need to cut price to sell additional units indicates downward-sloping firm demand. This is characteristic of imperfect competition in product markets.

prompt: If a firm can sell any feasible quantity at exactly $20 without changing price, the firm is more consistent with
explanation: Horizontal firm demand means the firm takes the market price as given. It is the perfect-competition benchmark.

prompt: A market with high start-up costs, legal restrictions, and control of key resources would likely have
explanation: Large start-up costs, legal restrictions, and exclusive resource control can each obstruct rival entry. All three can sustain market power.

prompt: Which statement about imperfect competition is most accurate?

options.label: C
options.text: It refers only to factor markets

options.label: D
options.text: It requires firms to be price takers

options.label: E
options.text: Different structures sharing some market power

explanation: Imperfect competition includes several structures with market power. Monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, and monopsony differ in how that power arises.

prompt: When an imperfectly competitive market produces where P>MC, the price signal

options.label: C
options.text: Shows that marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit

options.label: E
options.text: Leaves some mutually beneficial trades unrealized

explanation: Price above MC means the next units are valued more than they cost. Forgoing them leaves positive gains from trade unrealized.

options.label: A

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: The firm faces perfectly elastic demand

options.label: E
options.text: The firm has no discretion over price

prompt: A firm increases sales from 40 to 50 units only after lowering price from $25 to $22. Which conclusion is most directly supported?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm is a pure price taker

options.label: B
options.text: There are no barriers to entry

options.label: C
options.text: The market must be perfectly competitive

options.label: A
options.text: Output is above the efficient quantity

options.label: E

prompt: At an output of 200 units, price is $15 and marginal cost is also $15. Relative to allocative efficiency, this condition is

options.label: C
options.text: Evidence that price is too high

explanation: At P = MC, the last unit's valuation equals its opportunity cost. This is allocative efficiency.

prompt: At an output of 75 units, price is $24 while MC is $16. Which statement best describes the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: The market must be perfectly competitive

options.label: D
options.text: The firm is necessarily productively efficient

options.label: E
options.text: Resources used on the marginal unit exceed consumer value

explanation: Price on the demand curve measures marginal benefit. P above MC therefore means the marginal value exceeds marginal cost.

prompt: Which industry is most likely to have a strong high-start-up-cost barrier?

options.label: B

options.label: D

options.label: E

explanation: The large up-front expenditure must be committed before sales occur. This financial hurdle can discourage entrants.

prompt: A city allows only firms with a limited government franchise to provide a particular service. This is most directly an example of
explanation: Government authorization restricts the right to operate. It is a legal barrier to entry.

prompt: One company owns exclusive rights to a rare input necessary to make a product. The most direct effect is to

options.label: A
options.text: Make every firm a price taker

explanation: Exclusive ownership denies rivals access to a key input. This is a resource-based barrier to entry.

prompt: A market has three large firms, each with some ability to affect market price. Which broad classification best fits the market?

options.label: A
options.text: Perfectly contestable with no market power

explanation: Some ability to influence price or market outcomes means the firm has market power. This differs from pure price taking.

options.label: D

options.label: E
options.text: The second firm has market power

prompt: Which pair contains only imperfectly competitive product-market structures?
explanation: Monopoly and oligopoly both involve seller market power. Both are imperfectly competitive product markets.

prompt: Which pair contains one imperfect product market and one imperfect factor market?
explanation: Oligopoly concerns market power among a few product sellers. Monopsony concerns buyer power in a factor market.

prompt: A new entrant would need to spend $500 million before earning any revenue, while incumbent firms already own the necessary infrastructure. This most directly illustrates
explanation: A large initial investment exposes entrants to a substantial financial commitment. It can deter them from entering.

prompt: A government removes a licensing requirement that previously limited who could operate in an industry. Other things equal, this change should
explanation: Removing the legal requirement eliminates one obstacle to starting operations. Entry becomes easier.

options.label: C

prompt: A potential entrant can obtain every needed input except one, which is controlled entirely by an incumbent. The primary obstacle is

prompt: Why can barriers to entry help sustain imperfect competition over time?

options.label: D

prompt: A market outcome has P=$45, MC=$30, and current quantity 1,000. The efficient quantity is 1,250 where P=MC. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The efficient quantity must be below 1,000

options.label: B
options.text: Quantity cannot be compared using P and MC

options.label: C
options.text: The current market overproduces by 250 units

options.label: D
options.text: The current market is efficient because P>MC

explanation: Efficient output is 1,250 compared with current output of 1,000. The market underproduces by 250 units.

prompt: A firm charges $45 per unit and has marginal cost of $30 at its current output. What is the price–marginal-cost wedge?
explanation: The price-cost gap is $45 - $30 = $15 per unit.

prompt: A firm's individual demand schedule is P=$60 at Q=10, $55 at Q=20, $50 at Q=30, and $45 at Q=40. Which inference is valid without using future Topic 4.2 rules?

options.label: B
options.text: The firm is definitely a monopoly

options.label: C
options.text: The firm's economic profit is positive

options.label: D
options.text: Downward-sloping demand gives it market power

explanation: The schedule shows that increasing sales requires cutting price. That supports a market-power inference without identifying the profit-maximizing output.

prompt: Which inference would go beyond Topic 4.1 if given only a downward-sloping firm demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Concluding that the firm must lower price to sell more

options.label: B
options.text: Recognizing that the firm has some market power

options.label: C
options.text: Classifying the market broadly as imperfectly competitive

options.label: D
options.text: Contrasting its demand with a price-taking firm's horizontal demand

options.label: E
options.text: Determining the monopoly profit-maximizing quantity using MR=MC

explanation: Demand alone does not provide the cost information needed to locate monopoly MR = MC. Determining that specific output goes beyond the broad characteristics given here.

options.label: D

prompt: A market produces 500 units where P=$36 and MC=$24. If the next units up to 600 have MB>MC, what does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: Price must be below marginal cost

options.label: C
options.text: The market is already allocatively efficient

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing output below 500 increases surplus necessarily

options.label: E
options.text: There are no unexploited gains from trade

explanation: When MB exceeds MC, the extra unit creates more value than it uses in resources. Additional output increases total surplus.

prompt: A market produces where P>MC even though potential entrants observe possible profits. Which Topic 4.1 explanation could account for market power persisting?

options.label: D
options.text: Perfectly elastic firm demand prevents entry

explanation: Profits can encourage entry without making entry feasible. Barriers can still prevent rivals from challenging market power.

prompt: Potential entrants would like to enter an industry, but a combination of patents, licensing, and exclusive input contracts blocks them. Which conclusion is strongest?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple barriers can sustain market power

options.label: B
options.text: The market must become perfectly competitive

options.label: D
options.text: The incumbent must face perfectly elastic demand

explanation: Legal protection and resource control can both restrict rivals. Their combined effect can sustain market power.

prompt: A firm lowers price from $50 to $45 when increasing sales from 100 to 130 units. Which statement about the firm's price-setting environment is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Its output choice has no connection to price

options.label: B
options.text: Output choices affect its selling price

options.label: C
options.text: It must accept one fixed market price

options.label: E
options.text: It faces a perfectly horizontal demand curve

explanation: The downward-sloping curve links the firm's price with its sales. More sales require a lower price.

prompt: A firm can increase sales without changing price, while another must lower price to sell more. Which statement best compares them?

options.label: A
options.text: The second is necessarily a monopoly

options.label: B
options.text: Both must have identical market power

options.label: C
options.text: The first firm is more consistent with imperfect competition

options.label: D
options.text: The second firm has market power

options.label: E
options.text: The first necessarily faces a legal entry barrier

explanation: A price taker faces horizontal demand at the market price. An imperfectly competitive seller faces downward-sloping individual demand.

prompt: Why does a P>MC outcome imply that the price mechanism is not coordinating all possible market participants efficiently?

options.label: B
options.text: All consumers value the product less than its cost

options.label: C
options.text: Marginal cost is greater than marginal benefit for unproduced units

options.label: D
options.text: Unproduced units have MB above MC

options.label: E
options.text: Every possible gain from trade is exhausted

explanation: The forgone units have benefits above production costs. Failing to trade them leaves mutually beneficial exchanges unrealized.

prompt: A firm is protected by a legal restriction on entry. If that restriction expires but the industry's start-up cost remains extremely high, what is the best prediction from Topic 4.1 alone?

options.label: B
options.text: The incumbent must lose all market power instantly

options.label: C
options.text: Price must immediately equal marginal cost

options.label: D
options.text: Entry remains exactly as difficult for exactly the same reasons

options.label: E
options.text: High start-up costs can still deter entry

explanation: Removing one barrier does not automatically remove another. A remaining restriction can continue to obstruct entry.

prompt: A market has four firms. This fact alone is insufficient to classify it because

options.label: A
options.text: The number of firms never matters in economics

options.label: B
options.text: All four-firm markets have horizontal firm demand

options.label: C
options.text: Any four-firm market is a monopoly

options.label: D
options.text: Any four-firm market is perfectly competitive

options.label: E
options.text: Market power, firm demand, and entry conditions

explanation: Firm numbers alone do not fully establish market power. Demand conditions, differentiation, and entry barriers also matter.

prompt: Which statement most accurately synthesizes Topic 4.1?

options.label: A
options.text: All imperfectly competitive firms are monopolies

options.label: C
options.text: Barriers to entry are irrelevant to persistent market power

options.label: D
options.text: Market power can create P > MC and underproduction

options.label: E
options.text: Imperfect competition is defined only by the number of firms

explanation: Imperfect competition involves market power and, for sellers, downward-sloping individual demand. Entry barriers can sustain it, and P above MC can leave output allocatively inefficient.
reference: PRD-3.B | PRD-3.B.1-4 Quality-Control Audits Audit 1 — CED Alignment and Scope All 100 questions are restricted to Topic 4.1 and PRD-3.B(a), using only Essential Knowledge PRD-3.B.1 through PRD-3.B.4. Coverage includes the four imperfectly competitive market structures named in the CED; the requirement that an imperfectly competitive output firm lower price to sell additional units; the inefficiency condition P > MC; and barriers to entry such as high fixed/start-up costs, legal barriers, and exclusive ownership of key resources. Graphs are included throughout the bank where appropriate: firm-demand comparisons, downward-sloping imperfect-firm demand, P > MC inefficiency relative to the MB=MC benchmark, start-up-cost barriers, and exclusive-resource-control barriers. Future Topic 4.2 content is deliberately excluded. No question requires monopoly profit maximization, MR=MC monopoly equilibrium, natural monopoly, monopoly profit/loss areas, or deadweight-loss calculations. Audit 2 — Construction, Difficulty, and Answer Integrity Question count: 100. Difficulty distribution: 33 Easy, 40 Medium, 27 Hard. Every item has five answer choices and exactly one keyed answer. Correct-answer positions are balanced exactly: A=20, B=20, C=20, D=20, E=20. Easy items focus on identification and core definitions. Medium items apply the concepts to demand schedules, entry-barrier scenarios, and P-MC efficiency reasoning. Hard items integrate multiple Topic 4.1 concepts while explicitly avoiding later monopoly-specific decision rules. All quantitative questions were recomputed during generation. P-MC wedges use simple subtraction, and allocative-efficiency items consistently apply the CED benchmark P=MC (equivalently MB=MC on the relevant demand/marginal-benefit curve).
